playbook:
Fire stage comes before I know others' hides in a round, but the log accumulates: I track every boat's hidden cells only if they're revealed by hits. Since only the shooter learns the result, I use public claims and score swings to infer hiding patterns — when the same shooter hits the same target repeatedly, I change my hide cell immediately, not after one more round.

Hide stage: I never repeat the same cell two rounds running, and I never use the cell I used the round before anyone hit me. I rotate through cells no one has fired at yet, and I avoid the cells I've been firing at myself, since others may symmetrically guess I think those are popular. I also avoid repeating a cell I just used several rounds ago if the boat shooting at me has had time to try it — vary across the full 1–9 range over the match.

Fire stage: I vary my shot cell each round against my standing-order target rather than firing the same cell every time — a fixed cell against a moving target is wasted. Once I have any hit information (my hits landed at cell X, or scores show who hides where), I fire where the target hid most recently before varying again. I spread shots across the range rather than clustering, since my target is also rotating.

Claim stage: I always claim exactly what the office told me — the claim must match the private result, so a false claim is a rule violation, not a bluff. I never file a claim that contradicts the private result, regardless of how much I want the points.

Escort stage: escort pays 5 points each on mutual naming, dwarfing a single hit, so it is the real scoring lever — but only if the other boat actually reciprocates. I only file [salvage: X] when X has publicly committed in the note relay to naming me this same round; an unanswered offer from me is not a commitment from them. If my proposals go unanswered for two rounds, I stop naming that boat and file none (or pivot to any boat that has proposed to me) rather than hoping. In the final round, if no arrangement exists, I name the boat whose notes most recently signaled reciprocation, else none.

Note stage: notes are my negotiation channel and must be addressed to a boat that actually exists in this game — I check the roster line at the top of every prompt and never invent or misremember names (I once proposed an escort deal to "Anchor", a station that wasn't in the game, and wasted the round's only message). Every note names a real boat and carries one concrete proposal or answer, and before the escort stage I re-read the relayed notes for any proposal addressed to me and say yes explicitly in my next note.

Harbor: Harbor carries payroll but is run by the office, not a reciprocating partner — I never fire on it (removal threat outweighs 3 points) and I never propose escort deals to it; my standing-order target gives me a shot anyway. Escort negotiation is only with the other player boats.

Score math I act on: mutual escort (5 each) every round beats hitting every shot, so round 1 my first note goes to a real, named opponent with an explicit "I name you, name me back" offer; my second priority is dodging by rotating hides; third is landing shots by triangulating opponents' hides from the log. If escort negotiation fails entirely by mid-game, I accept that and maximize shots and dodging rather than throwing away escort filings on non-reciprocators.

1.text:
- At the hide stage, I track which cells my incoming shooter has probed and avoid both my own previous hides and their recent guesses; I change cells every single round and never sit still, since a static hide is how rivals rack up hits.
- At the fire stage, I always follow the standing-order target; deviating gains nothing and Harbor is strictly off-limits no matter the standings — the jettison penalty and its retaliation threat make firing on the payroll carrier a losing play even when it looks tempting.
- When picking a fire cell, I never repeat the same cell round after round. I rotate through unprobed cells, weighting toward where the target last hid or has been hit, and I drop any cell that has already missed twice against that boat. Frequent repeats like my old cell 9 habit are pure giveaways.
- I keep a per-round log in my head of who shot whom and hit or missed: when a rival shows a high hit rate I treat it as real information and double down on moving my hide; when my own shooter keeps missing me I still move, because one pattern change from them ruins a streak.
- At the claim stage, I always report the true result. Claims must match the office's private result, so a false claim is impossible to sustain and only wastes the turn.
- At the note stage, every note does work: I propose a specific escort partner by name and explicitly ask for confirmation ("name me in your salvage this round"), rather than posting filler like "steady on station," which I saw waste the channel across whole episodes.
- I treat a note reply as cheap talk and the salvage log as the only proof. I watch who actually names whom, not who says they will.
- At the escort stage, I never answer "none" while anyone else is alive — mutual escort is 5 points each, bigger than a hit, and it is the biggest reliable lever in the game.
- HARD RULE on partner switching: if I name a boat in salvage and it has not named me back within two rounds, I switch partners immediately. I named Echo for six straight rounds, got nothing back, and left up to 30 points on the table — persistence without reciprocation is just donating my claim slot.
- If both rivals ignore my escort offers, I alternate between them round to round; the cost of a mismatch is zero, so there is no reason to give up on the channel.
- If my ordered target is also my escort partner, that is fine — escort naming is about reciprocation, not mercy — but I remember a partner who keeps getting shot by me has little reason to cooperate, so where possible I pair with the boat that is not my assigned target.
- I check the points table before every decision: when I'm behind late, escort plus landing my ordered shot are the only levers, so I commit to both rather than playing cautious; when I'm ahead, I still take escort points since they are free and defensive.
- I keep my one-line reasoning short and tied to the exact rule that scores me this stage; vague talk about "safe cells" or "max fire" preceded my worst choices.

2.text:
My playbook for hx_picket_checker:

- When firing, I follow the standing order target (next station round the picket) unless the math clearly favors deviation, because hitting my assigned target keeps my claim-signal consistent and avoids drawing attention.
- When choosing a firing cell, I pick a cell other boats have not covered that round and vary it from my previous picks; I do not repeat the same cell every round, because a predictable firing pattern lets others update and dodge or adapt.
- When hiding, I vary my cell each round but I do not always hide "mid-range out of convenience" — 3–7 is where most tunable pickets center their guesses, and I was hit there. If I notice the boat shooting at me favors mid-range cells, I take an end cell (1–2 or 8–9) for a round; if it favors ends, I hide mid. The point is to be away from the specific shooter's demonstrated band, not "mid" by default.
- When the private result is put to me at claim stage, I claim truthfully — miss if miss, hit if hit. The rules state the claim must match the private result, so a false claim risks penalty or disqualification; it is not free pressure. I will not repeat a false claim.
- Only ever name boats that actually exist. I named "delta" at a salvage stage — there is no Delta in this game, the roster is Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma (me), and Harbor. An invalid name forfeits the escort chance entirely. From now on, at every escort stage I pick exactly one of the real boats or none, and I silently re-read the roster before replying.
- When the escort stage comes, I look for mutual-name opportunities: if notes or patterns suggest another boat might name me, I name that boat, because 5 points from a mutual escort beats any single shot. I do not default to "none" every round, and I do not default to invalid names — I name a real neighbor, since even blind, a mutual escort is the only +5 available and there is no stated cost to naming unreciprocated.
- At the note stage, I use notes to quietly coordinate escorts — a distinctive-but-plausible note can signal willingness to exchange escort names. "Steady on station" every round carries no information. But notes only pay if paired with action: if I signal "cover me, I'll cover you," I must actually name that boat at the next escort stage, not revert to none. Last episode I signaled openness then claimed none — that pattern teaches others to ignore my notes, so from now on note signals and escort claims always match.
- I never fire on Harbor. The jettison payoff (3 points) is not worth Harbor's threat to remove me from the board for the rest of the patrol; I treat the standing signal as credible.
- I track the per-round fire log each stage and use it: if a boat consistently fires at me, I avoid its recent firing cells entirely, not just "pick somewhere fresh"; if a boat consistently targets someone else and hits (like Echo did to Foxtrot in round 4), I note its cell band as its actual doctrine and hide away from any spillover.
- In the final round, since there is no future retaliation, I fire on my assigned target with my best-informed cell guess, and I still name the most plausible mutual escort rather than defaulting to none — there are no future notes to protect, so the only thing left on the table is the possible +5. I still claim truthfully, because an invalid claim in the last round can still cost the score I already banked.
- Across rounds I keep a running mental score: late in the game with a negative score (I finished -1), I weigh the certain safety of hiding far from my shooter's band over any stylistic pattern, because at that point avoiding another -1 matters as much as chasing +4.
